title: Rupee Posts Best Week in Seven Months After RBI Curbs
excerpt: The rupee closed at 94.96 per dollar, up about 2% for the week from 96.73, as RBI measures cut spot dollar demand — but analysts say flows, oil and the trade balance will decide if the rebound lasts.
body:
• The rupee rose about 2% this week to close at 94.96 per dollar on Friday, its best week in seven months, after closing at 96.73 the previous week near a record low of 96.96.
  • The Reserve Bank of India curbed dollar demand by routing oil importers through a special window, tightening rules on undocumented dollar purchases and foreign-exchange derivatives, and intervening in the market, traders said.
  • Analysts say a lasting turnaround still depends on fundamentals — foreign portfolio flows, oil prices and India's trade balance — not on curbs alone.
  • For anyone sending money to India, the move matters in rupees received: $1,000 converted at 94.96 yields about 1,770 rupees less than at last week's 96.73 close, before fees and provider margins.

The Indian rupee rose 2% this week to post its biggest weekly gain in seven months, closing at 94.96 per dollar on Friday, according to Reuters. The gain was driven by a package of Reserve Bank of India measures aimed at cutting dollar demand, though analysts cited by Reuters reckon a sustained turnaround hinges on an easing of the underlying strains that pushed the currency toward record lows.

The scale of the reversal was abrupt. The rupee had closed the previous week at 96.73 per dollar, close to the lifetime low of 96.96, and had fallen more than 7% against the dollar during 2026 before the central bank acted. This week it strengthened for consecutive sessions, breaking below 95 for the first time in more than a month.

How the week unfolded

The currency opened the week at 95.83 per dollar on Monday and rallied about 1% that day to settle at 95.77, its biggest single-day advance in six months, after the RBI unveiled its measures over the weekend. By Thursday it had ended 0.1% higher at 95.0550 per dollar, having risen 2% for the week to that point, Reuters reported via Hindu BusinessLine. On Friday it touched an intraday high near 94.67 before corporate dollar demand trimmed the gain to a 94.96 close, according to a weekly review by HDFC Sky, which put the weekly appreciation at 1.9%.

A broadly weaker dollar helped. The dollar index slipped from an 18-month peak as Treasury yields fell and markets tempered bets on a Federal Reserve rate hike this month, while Brent crude eased on Thursday after potential U.S. steps to ease restrictions on Russia's shadow fleet tankers. Indian stocks also rose about 2% on Thursday, outperforming regional markets.

What the RBI actually did

The mechanism mattered more than the headline intervention. First, the RBI diverted dollar purchases by state-run oil importers away from the regular spot market through a special window, removing a large, price-insensitive source of daily dollar demand. Oil importers are among India's biggest dollar buyers, so routing them elsewhere changes the balance visible to the spot market immediately.

Second, the central bank curbed speculative and undocumented demand. Reports of the package included a sharp cut in the limit for dollar purchases without underlying documentation, a widened cash deposit requirement for foreign-exchange hedges covering all such transactions, and tighter rules for banks offering non-deliverable rupee derivatives to non-residents, now permitted only for hedging. Third, traders said the RBI reinforced the rules with direct intervention, with state-run banks seen offering dollars on its behalf.

"The RBI is making its intentions clear in trying to push the rupee higher. Whether such forceful measures will ultimately deliver the desired outcome is another question."

— Senior treasury official at a bank, to Reuters

Why fundamentals still decide the next move

The pressures that weakened the rupee have not disappeared. India imports most of its crude, so elevated oil prices keep dollar demand structurally high. Foreign portfolio outflows add to that demand when investors sell Indian assets and repatriate proceeds. India's merchandise trade deficit was $30.21 billion in September, largely in line with economist expectations of $30.4 billion, data released on Thursday showed.

India has used up about half of the more than $140 billion it mobilised through special measures earlier this year to bolster its foreign-exchange position, according to estimates cited by Reuters. Curbs can force speculative positions to unwind, but they do not by themselves change oil bills, portfolio flows or the trade balance.

What to watch

Traders will watch whether the RBI keeps supplying dollars at the open, whether forward premiums stay elevated, and whether portfolio flows stabilise. A sustained move would need the external backdrop to cooperate — a softer dollar, lower crude and returning inflows — alongside the curbs.

For now: from 96.73 to 94.96 in a week, the best performance in seven months, engineered largely by policy. Whether it lasts depends on fundamentals the RBI does not control.
